questions.q: What distinguishes test-time compute methods (best-of-n, self-consistency, search) from the RLVR training covered earlier in this chapter?
options: They require retraining the policy's weights from scratch
They improve answer quality by spending additional inference-time compute on a fixed, already-trained policy, with no change to the model's weights
They are a replacement for the policy's reward model during training
They only work on models that have never been trained with RL
questions.explain: Test-time compute methods operate entirely at inference, sampling or searching more from a fixed policy, rather than updating the policy's parameters.

questions.q: Why does self-consistency not require a separate scorer or reward model, unlike best-of-n?
options: It only works on code problems

It extracts the final answer from each of several independent reasoning paths and takes a majority vote, relying on the fact that independent reasoning errors tend not to agree while correct paths tend to converge
It always generates exactly one sample
It uses the same verifier as best-of-n but calls it differently
questions.explain: Self-consistency only needs to extract and compare final answers across samples; the majority vote itself substitutes for an explicit scorer.

questions.q: How does PRM-guided search differ from best-of-n and self-consistency in what it evaluates?
options: It only evaluates the prompt, never the generated text
It scores and prunes partial, in-progress reasoning paths during generation, rather than only scoring completed traces after they are finished
It is identical to best-of-n in every respect
It requires no process reward model at all
questions.explain: PRM-guided search evaluates intermediate steps to abandon unpromising partial paths early, closer to tree search, while best-of-n and self-consistency only look at finished traces.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how do test-time compute methods and RLVR training relate to each other?
options: They are competing alternatives, and a team must choose only one

They are complementary: RLVR training raises the single-try base rate of a good trace, and test-time search multiplies further on top of an already-improved base rate, needing fewer samples as a result
Test-time compute makes RLVR training entirely unnecessary
RLVR training makes test-time compute methods impossible to use
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames the two as stacking levers rather than substitutes — a better-trained policy makes search cheaper, and search further improves on a better-trained policy's outputs.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say PRM labeling cost, which was too expensive for dense RL training signal per lesson 54, can still make sense for test-time search?
options: PRM labeling cost disappears entirely at inference time
A PRM used for search only needs to be applied to the much smaller number of queries that actually reach a user, rather than across millions of training rollouts
Search does not use a PRM at all, so cost is irrelevant
Test-time compute requires no PRM evaluation whatsoever
questions.explain: The cost-per-use tradeoff differs by scale: millions of RL rollouts make per-step PRM scoring expensive in training, while the smaller volume of real user queries makes the same PRM affordable as an inference-time search guide.
